about-page.subtitle: Why this question is harder than it looks
about-page.intro: This isn't a poll. It's a thought experiment with real stakes — a live version of one of the most studied problems in game theory: the coordination game.
about-page.setup.body: Every person who visits this site faces the same binary choice with no communication, no second chances, and consequences that depend entirely on what everyone else decides. The rules are simple:
about-page.setup.red-rule: Red majority — only those who pressed red survive.
about-page.setup.conclusion: Blue is better for the world. Red is safer for you — if you don't trust the world.
about-page.two-answers.body1: Game theorists would point out that red is the Nash equilibrium choice: the individually optimal move regardless of what others do. If more than half press blue, red pressers survive. If not, red pressers survive anyway. Red dominates as a personal strategy.
about-page.two-answers.body2: But blue is the Pareto-optimal outcome — the choice that minimises total harm if enough people make it. The catch is that blue only works if you trust that others will cooperate. And you have no way of knowing if they will.
about-page.two-answers.body3: Neither answer is irrational. Red-choosers are protecting themselves under genuine uncertainty. Blue-choosers are betting that trust is self-fulfilling — that if enough people reason the same way, the cooperative outcome becomes real.
about-page.viral.body1: The question keeps resurfacing because it maps onto almost every major collective problem humanity faces: vaccination, climate commitments, arms races, nuclear deterrence. In each case, the individually safe choice undermines the collectively good one — and vice versa.
about-page.viral.body2: The virality also reflects something about our moment. We're increasingly aware of global interdependence, increasingly uncertain about whether other people will cooperate, and increasingly drawn to thought experiments that force the question.
about-page.data.body1: Across surveys and viral polls, a consistent majority chooses blue — despite the logical case for red. The reasons vary: concern for loved ones, moral responsibility, optimism about human nature, or the simple belief that if you press blue, maybe enough others will too.
about-page.data.body2: Whether that optimism is rational or naive is exactly the question.

why-blue-page.subtitle: The case for cooperation
why-blue-page.intro: Blue is the harder choice. It requires trusting strangers — billions of them — without any guarantee they'll trust you back. Here's why that bet might be worth making.
why-blue-page.self-fulfilling.h2: If You Press Blue, Others Might Too
why-blue-page.self-fulfilling.body: Your choice doesn't happen in a vacuum. Millions of people are facing this exact question, reasoning through it the same way you are. If your logic leads you to blue, it's likely leading others there too. Blue is self-fulfilling in a way red isn't — the more people reason toward cooperation, the more cooperation becomes the rational choice.
why-blue-page.collective.body: Blue is the Pareto-optimal outcome: the only scenario where total survival is maximised. Red can only "win" by making blue lose. There's no version of a red majority where the world is better off than it would have been under a blue majority.
why-blue-page.red-unsafe.body: Red feels safe because it avoids the worst individual outcome — dying in a blue failure. But if red wins, people die. If you press red and red wins, you survived by being part of the group that caused everyone else's death. The "safety" of red is conditional on others' suffering.
why-blue-page.majority.body1: Across every version of this question that's gone viral, a clear majority chooses blue. The reasons range from moral responsibility to optimism about human nature to concern for loved ones. Whatever the motivation, the revealed preference of humanity in this experiment has consistently leaned cooperative.
why-blue-page.majority.body2: If most people press blue, pressing red is a defection — taking the benefit of others' cooperation while refusing to offer it yourself.
why-blue-page.schelling.body: Game theorists call it a Schelling point: a solution people converge on without communication, simply because it's the obvious focal one. "Cooperate" is the natural focal point when the cooperative outcome is unambiguously better for everyone. Blue doesn't need a coordinated campaign — it just needs enough people to reason the same way.
why-red-page.subtitle: The case for self-preservation
why-red-page.intro: Red is the uncomfortable choice to defend — it sounds selfish. But the logic behind it is precise, and dismissing it as irrational misses the point of the dilemma.
why-red-page.nash.body: In game theory, a Nash equilibrium is a choice where you can't do better by switching, given what everyone else does. Red is that choice here: if more than half press blue, red pressers survive. If more than half press red, red pressers survive. Red dominates as an individual strategy regardless of what the majority does.
why-red-page.uncertainty.h2: You Can't Know What Others Will Do
why-red-page.uncertainty.body1: Blue only works if the majority cooperates. But you have no information about what the other billions of people are pressing. The rational response to genuine uncertainty is to choose the option that protects you across more scenarios — and that's red.
why-red-page.uncertainty.body2: Pressing blue because you assume others will press blue is optimism posing as logic. It might be right. It might not be. Red doesn't require that assumption.
why-red-page.framing.h2: The Framing Is Doing a Lot of Work
why-red-page.framing.body: Reframe the same question: a blender activates and kills you unless a majority of strangers also step into blenders. Would you step in? Almost no one would — yet the payoff structure is identical. The blue button sounds cooperative because it's framed that way. Strip the framing and you're being asked to stake your life on the goodwill of people you've never met and can't communicate with.
why-red-page.villain.h2: Choosing Red Doesn't Make You the Villain
why-red-page.villain.body1: If red wins, it's because the majority pressed red — not because one person did. An individual red press in a blue-majority world costs nothing and saves no one. An individual red press in a red-majority world saves exactly one person: you.
why-red-page.villain.body2: Red-choosers aren't causing harm. They're responding rationally to a system that doesn't reward trust with certainty.
why-red-page.distrust.body: The real-world parallels to this dilemma — arms races, climate commitments, collective action problems — have a mixed track record at best. People who've watched cooperative frameworks collapse, been betrayed by institutions, or simply grown up in environments where trust was a liability aren't being irrational when they press red. They're applying a prior built from experience.
privacy-page.subtitle: Last updated: May 5, 2026
privacy-page.intro: This privacy policy describes how redor.blue ("we", "us") handles information when you use our website.
privacy-page.collect.intro: When you cast a vote, we record:
privacy-page.collect.item2: Your country, derived from your IP address
privacy-page.collect.item3: A one-way SHA-256 hash of your IP address, used solely to prevent duplicate votes. Your raw IP address is never stored.
privacy-page.cookies.intro: We store two cookies in your browser:
privacy-page.cookies.voted-text: records that you have already voted, so we can redirect you to the results page
privacy-page.cookies.choice-text: remembers your choice (red or blue) to show your personal outcome
privacy-page.cookies.outro: These cookies contain no personal information and are not used for tracking or advertising.
privacy-page.adsense.body: We use Google AdSense to display advertisements. Google may use cookies and collect data about your browsing activity to serve personalised ads. This is governed by <googlePrivacy>Google's Privacy Policy</googlePrivacy>. You can opt out of personalised advertising via <adSettings>Google's Ad Settings</adSettings>.
privacy-page.sharing.body: We do not sell, trade, or share your data with any third party, except as described above (Google AdSense).
privacy-page.retention.body: Vote data (choice, country, and hashed IP) is retained indefinitely for the purpose of displaying aggregate results. No personally identifiable information is stored.
privacy-page.contact.body: If you have any questions about this policy, you can reach us at <email>privacy@redor.blue</email>.
